title: Russia doubles its 2026 deficit forecast as oil revenue falls 17%
deck: Moscow's budget now assumes a deficit nearly twice the plan, a record defence bill and $50 oil, and that squeeze gives the Kremlin more reasons to push for diplomacy and higher OPEC+ quotas.

card.headline: Russia's war economy is running hot on spending and cold on oil revenue

keyNumber.label: projected 2026 deficit ($88bn, 3.2% of GDP), against 3.785 trillion originally planned

forYou.line: Watch how Moscow funds a gap that is nearly double the plan; the mix of borrowing, reserves and taxes is not yet clear.
Russia needs higher prices and quotas. Expect it to defend its 9.9 mb/d share at the OPEC+ meeting on 1 November.
A cash-strapped state tends to raise taxes and squeeze civilian budgets. Review payment, contract and tax risk.
A third of spending on defence and a thinning revenue base raise the odds that Moscow seeks a deal, or digs in and pays for it elsewhere.

effects.text: The 2026 deficit forecast rises to 7.345 trillion rubles from 3.785 trillion planned
The January-September deficit already hit 5.2 trillion rubles, about 71% of the full-year forecast
Oil-and-gas revenue fell 17.2% while spending rose 14.5%
The 2027 defence budget rises 27% to a record 17.1 trillion rubles, more than a third of federal outlays
Pressure to fill the gap through borrowing, reserve drawdowns or new taxes (the mix is not stated in our sources)
Civilian spending on regions, health and education competes with a fast-growing defence line
A $50 oil baseline leaves room for upside if Brent stays near $100, but constrained flows have kept revenue falling
Moscow lobbies inside OPEC+ for higher quotas and prices
A stronger incentive to seek a Trump-Xi summit on a Ukraine deal
Less fiscal room to absorb a longer war or a new sanctions round
Higher domestic taxes or financing costs could squeeze Russian firms and households over 2027

whatHappened: On 1 October 2026 the Russian government sent a three-year budget to the State Duma. It projects a 2026 deficit of 7.345 trillion rubles ($88bn, or 3.2% of GDP). That is nearly double the 3.785 trillion originally planned.
The numbers were already moving. The Finance Ministry reported a January-September deficit of 5.2 trillion rubles ($61bn). Oil-and-gas revenue fell 17.2% while spending rose 14.5%.
The 2027 plan lifts defence spending 27% to a record 17.1 trillion rubles, more than a third of federal outlays. It assumes oil at $50 a barrel. The Duma's first reading is set for 29 October.
whyItMatters: Russia's war economy depends on energy revenue and state spending. When one falls and the other rises, the gap has to be funded. That limits how long Moscow can sustain this pace without hard trade-offs.
The squeeze comes even though Brent trades above $100, against $73 before the Gulf war began. Constrained Russian flows mean the price windfall is not reaching the budget.

The deficit links to two other live stories. It raises the Kremlin's incentive to seek a summit with Trump and Xi on Ukraine. It also shapes Russia's push inside OPEC+, where it wants to protect its 9.9 mb/d share.

winners.why: A record 17.1 trillion rubles in 2027 means more orders, whatever happens to the rest of the budget.

winners.who: OPEC+ members that gain from high prices
winners.why: Brent above $100 helps producers able to export, even as Russia's own receipts fall.

losers.why: With defence above a third of outlays, the other lines face competition for a shrinking pot (our inference; the sources give the totals, not the cuts).
Closing a deficit this size usually means new taxes or costlier state borrowing, though the mix has not been confirmed in our sources.

losers.who: The ruble and Russian state finances
losers.why: A bigger deficit and thinner oil revenue raise fiscal risk.

whatsNext: 29 October: Duma first reading of the 2026-2028 budget.
1 November: core OPEC+ producers meet again after holding November targets unchanged.
November: Finance Ministry's October data will show whether the deficit keeps widening.
Late 2026: final adoption of the budget, and a sign of whether the defence figure holds.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely fiscal path for Russia over the next six months?
options: Muddle through: pass the budget as drafted and fund the gap with borrowing and reserves
Sharp austerity on civilian spending and new tax rises
A windfall from oil or diplomacy closes the gap
A funding squeeze forces cuts to defence plans
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 50%, is muddle-through: the Duma passes the draft with little change and the gap is covered by borrowing, reserves and incremental taxes. The mix is our estimate, not a sourced fact. Tightening on civilian lines is the second most likely at 25%.

recap.question: What deficit does the budget project for 2026?
By how much did oil-and-gas revenue fall in January-September?
What oil price does the 2027 budget assume?

timeline.title: US and Israeli strikes on Iran begin
timeline.detail: Oil and freight costs stay elevated for eight months; Brent goes from $73 before the war to above $100.

timeline.title: Budget submitted to the Duma
timeline.detail: A three-year budget projects a 2026 deficit of 7.345 trillion rubles, nearly double the 3.785 trillion planned, and a 27% rise in 2027 defence spending to 17.1 trillion.

timeline.title: OPEC+ holds November targets
timeline.detail: Seven core producers, including Russia at 9.9 mb/d, keep targets unchanged and set their next meeting for 1 November.

timeline.title: Finance Ministry reports the nine-month deficit
timeline.detail: The January-September deficit reaches 5.2 trillion rubles ($61bn). Oil-and-gas revenue is down 17.2% and spending is up 14.5%.

timeline.title: Duma first reading scheduled
timeline.detail: The first formal test of the draft budget in the lower house.

timeline.title: Next OPEC+ core meeting
timeline.detail: Russia's lobbying for quotas and prices is likely to feature.

causes.name: Energy dependence
causes.detail: The federal budget leans on oil-and-gas revenue, so price and volume swings hit it quickly.

causes.name: War-driven spending
causes.detail: Defence has become a dominant claim on the budget, now more than a third of 2027 outlays.

causes.name: Sanctions and constrained flows
causes.detail: Even at high world prices, Russian export volumes and realised prices are limited.

causes.name: Revenue down, spending up
causes.detail: Oil-and-gas revenue fell 17.2% while spending rose 14.5%, producing a 5.2 trillion ruble deficit in nine months.

causes.name: Defence step-up
causes.detail: A 27% rise in 2027 defence spending to 17.1 trillion rubles locks in a high spending path.

causes.name: Conservative price baseline
causes.detail: The budget assumes $50 oil, far below the current market, which could flatter or distort the final outcome.

causes.name: Gulf war disruption
causes.detail: The energy shock raises prices but also disrupts routes and flows, so the benefit to Russia is partial.

stakeholders.name: The Kremlin and Vladimir Putin
stakeholders.role: Final decision-maker on war and budget priorities
stakeholders.wants: Sustain war spending without a visible fiscal crisis and secure a favourable Ukraine settlement
stakeholders.leverage: Control of the budget process, the Duma and the central bank
stakeholders.likelyMove: Protect defence, push for diplomacy on its own terms and avoid a public austerity debate

stakeholders.name: Finance Ministry
stakeholders.wants: A plan that closes with tolerable financing costs
stakeholders.leverage: Choice of financing mix and timing of spending
stakeholders.likelyMove: Rely on borrowing, reserves and incremental revenue measures (our estimate)

stakeholders.name: State Duma
stakeholders.leverage: Formal readings and amendments, little independent sway
stakeholders.likelyMove: Approve the draft after the 29 October reading with minor changes

stakeholders.name: Russian Central Bank
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold a cautious stance as deficit financing weighs on rates (our estimate)

stakeholders.name: OPEC+ partners, led by Saudi Arabia
stakeholders.leverage: Larger spare capacity and a delayed capacity review that shapes 2027 quotas
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep targets stable while the Gulf flows stay disrupted

stakeholders.name: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping
stakeholders.wants: Different things: Trump a deal, Xi stability and leverage
stakeholders.likelyMove: Engage selectively while Moscow's fiscal pressure strengthens Washington's hand

stakeholders.name: Ukraine and its backers
stakeholders.wants: Maintain support and tighten pressure on Russian finances
stakeholders.leverage: Aid, sanctions and strikes on energy infrastructure
stakeholders.likelyMove: Cite the deficit to argue that pressure is working

sectors.why: Defence spending rises 27% to 17.1 trillion rubles in 2027.
With defence above a third of outlays, other lines compete for less room (inference).
World prices are high, but the 17.2% revenue fall shows constrained flows and lower realised take.

sectors.sector: Russian government debt and the ruble
sectors.why: A near-doubled deficit raises financing needs and fiscal risk.
More state borrowing can absorb bank balance sheets, but higher yields help margins (inference).
Russia's push for higher quotas competes with the need to keep prices from choking demand.

dailyLife.effect: A deficit this large usually brings tax measures or tighter civilian budgets. The sources do not specify which.
Higher state borrowing and defence spending can keep interest rates and prices elevated (inference).
Brent above $100 versus $73 before the war; French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.
Expect payment delays, tax changes and tougher contract terms as the state seeks cash (inference).

scenarios.name: Muddle-through
scenarios.looksLike: The Duma passes the draft with small changes. The gap is financed with borrowing, reserves and incremental revenue measures. Defence stays near 17.1 trillion rubles.
signposts: Passage after the 29 October reading with limited amendments
Finance Ministry gives a clear financing plan
Deficit data in line with the 7.345 trillion forecast
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Russia sustains the war effort at a high fiscal cost, keeping pressure for a diplomatic exit while steady.

scenarios.name: Tightening
scenarios.looksLike: New tax rises and cuts to civilian programmes, with defence protected.
signposts: Slower civilian spending in monthly data
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Domestic strain rises; Moscow's bargaining position on Ukraine depends on how visible it becomes.

scenarios.name: Revenue relief
scenarios.looksLike: Higher export volumes, a quota increase or a diplomatic breakthrough eases the gap.
signposts: OPEC+ quota changes in Russia's favour
Oil-and-gas revenue turns positive year on year
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Russia gains breathing room and less urgency to compromise.

scenarios.name: Funding stress
scenarios.looksLike: Financing costs spike or reserves run low, forcing cuts to defence plans or emergency measures.
signposts: Abrupt revisions to the defence line
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A sharper shift in Moscow's war calculus, though it is hard to predict how.

predictions.text: The Duma passes the budget at first reading on or about 29 October. Probability 0.93.
The final 2027 defence line stays within 5% of 17.1 trillion rubles. Probability 0.85.
The full-year 2026 federal deficit, as reported by the Finance Ministry, ends above 7.345 trillion rubles. Probability 0.5.
No Putin-Trump-Xi summit takes place. Probability 0.9.

actions: Review contracts with Russian counterparties for payment-delay and tax-change risk.
Avoid assuming that high oil prices will stabilise Russian customers' finances.
Track Russian tax proposals as they move through the Duma.
Watch monthly Finance Ministry deficit data against the 7.345 trillion forecast.
Treat Russian sovereign and bank risk as higher until the financing mix is clear.
Follow the 1 November OPEC+ meeting for signs Russia is winning quota concessions.
Expect fuel prices to stay elevated while Gulf flows are disrupted.
Do not read the Russian deficit as a quick path to lower energy prices.
Consider the deficit when judging how sanctions and energy measures bite.
Prepare for Moscow to push summit diplomacy while it is under fiscal pressure.
Coordinate on OPEC+ and Gulf supply risks, which shape Russian revenue.

analogues.event: 2014-16 oil price collapse and ruble crisis
analogues.whatFollowed: Russia drew heavily on its Reserve Fund, which was largely exhausted by about 2017, and tightened budgets.
A deficit of roughly 4% of GDP, financed by borrowing and reserves, then a return to surpluses as oil recovered.
Lower oil earnings strained Soviet finances and contributed to later pressure for economic and political change.

watch.title: Duma first reading
watch.why: Shows whether the draft passes unchanged and how the financing mix is described.

watch.title: OPEC+ core meeting
watch.why: Russia's push for higher quotas and prices tests its leverage.

watch.title: Monthly Finance Ministry deficit data
watch.why: Tells whether the 7.345 trillion rubles forecast is holding or will be overshot.

watch.title: Brent against the $50 budget baseline
watch.why: The gap between the market and the baseline shapes how much windfall revenue is possible.

watch.title: Ukraine summit diplomacy
watch.why: The fiscal squeeze raises the Kremlin's incentive to seek a deal.

confidence.note: From the event summary; we did not open the full articles.

confidence.note: From the event summary; not independently checked.

Author judgement, to be graded as events resolve.

evidence.method: Drafted from the two listed sources (a Moscow Times budget report and a TASS Finance Ministry report) and their headlines, plus the event summary and the three linked events. We did not read the full articles. The fiscal figures come from the summary and headlines. The financing mix, sector effects, stakeholder moves, scenario probabilities and predictions are our estimates, as are the historical analogues, which are from general knowledge and approximate.
